summary: This benchmark evaluates whether a frozen 2,306-parameter routing mechanism pretrained on single-hop register reads can be transplanted across distinct host architectures (temporal convolution vs. GRU) to follow multi-hop write chains. The experimental design is exceptionally disciplined, featuring rigorous baselines (native scratch training and matched one-hop pretraining) and causal intervention audits, though the scope is restricted to synthetic toy lookup tasks.
strengths: Methodologically rigorous comparison isolating the benefit of learned routing weights using both lower-bound (scratch) and upper-bound (matched one-hop pretraining) baselines.
Comprehensive causal intervention analysis (evaluating current-link vs. obsolete-link edits and rolling score controls) to test if the hosts legitimately use the router's outputs.

Transparent reporting of experimental verification, including an input audit that caught and corrected generator anomalies, along with exact software versions (Python 3.12.16, MLX 0.32.4, NumPy 2.5.5) and hardware runtime metrics.
weaknesses: The evaluation is confined to small synthetic register-alias tables with 2,306 routing parameters, leaving the transferability of modular routers in real-world large language models untested.
The frozen transplant is not evaluated under target fine-tuning, meaning the comparison conflates weight freezing with transplant viability.
The text is dense and assumes deep familiarity with the author's previous 'address_study' setup, making standalone comprehension challenging.
suggestions: Include an ablation where the transplanted donor weights are fine-tuned on the target task at the same update budget to decouple architecture transfer from parameter freezing.
Expand evaluation to standard synthetic reasoning benchmarks or larger sequence-to-sequence transformers to test generalizability beyond small GRU and temporal conv hosts.
Provide clearer schematics and definitions of the alias table structure and soft composition mechanism directly in the text.

claims.text: Pointer Networks [arXiv:1506.03134] introduced sequence-to-sequence models that use attention as pointers to select elements of an input sequence as discrete outputs.
Associative recall tasks [arXiv:2312.04927] serve as foundational benchmarks for evaluating in-context memory, indirect retrieval, and state tracking in sequence architectures.
Across four fits, the frozen graft answered 58.6–63.3% of held-out queries compared to 2.2–2.4% for native routers trained from scratch under the same 128-update budget.
claims.source: Internal mathematical consistency across reported fits (Convolution: 58.84% and 58.59% vs 2.45% and 2.37%; GRU: 63.17% and 63.26% vs 2.25% and 2.38%)

novelty_vs_existing.title: Pointer Networks
novelty_vs_existing.contribution: While Pointer Networks established data-driven selection of variable-length sequence elements, this benchmark tests whether learned pointer/routing submodules can be frozen and transplanted across structurally distinct host architectures (Conv vs. GRU).

novelty_vs_existing.title: Zoology: Measuring and Improving Recall in Efficient Language Models
novelty_vs_existing.contribution: Extends synthetic associative recall concepts to multi-hop alias chains and benchmarks cross-architecture modular weight grafting rather than standalone model capacity.
